lesson.title: The Promise Behind the Protocol
lesson.summary: A service model is the abstract guarantee a layer or protocol offers to whatever uses it, describing what it promises to deliver rather than how it accomplishes that delivery, and it is what actually distinguishes protocols like TCP and UDP from each other.
lesson.body:
A protocol, as covered earlier in this material, is a set of precise rules governing the format and meaning of messages exchanged between systems. The service model is a related but distinct idea: it is the abstract contract a protocol offers to whoever uses it, stated purely in terms of what is guaranteed, not how that guarantee is achieved internally. Two protocols can implement wildly different mechanisms, sequence numbers, timers, acknowledgment schemes, and still offer the same service model to the layer above them, or conversely, two protocols with similar mechanisms can offer very different service models depending on what they choose to guarantee.

This distinction matters because an application programmer, or a layer above a given protocol, generally does not need to know the internal mechanics of how a guarantee is kept. What they need to know is the service model: will my data arrive in order, will it arrive at all, will duplicate copies ever appear, is a connection required before I send anything. Answering these questions is what lets a programmer choose the right tool for a task without becoming an expert in the low level mechanics of retransmission timers or window scaling.

A useful analogy is two delivery companies. One company requires a customer to schedule a pickup in advance, tracks every package with a barcode scanned at each stop, requires a signature on delivery, and reships anything that is lost. The other company simply accepts a stack of postcards, drops each one in the nearest mailbox, and offers no tracking or guarantee that any particular postcard arrives. The service model is the promise printed on each company's brochure: tracked, signature confirmed delivery versus untracked, no guarantee delivery. The actual trucks, routes, and sorting facilities each company uses internally are the protocol mechanics, and a customer choosing between them cares about the brochure's promise, not the internal logistics.

In networking, this exact distinction plays out at the transport layer between TCP and UDP, and it is worth naming precisely here because the next several concepts build directly on it. TCP's service model promises reliable, ordered, byte stream delivery between two endpoints that have established a connection. UDP's service model promises none of that: it offers unordered, unacknowledged delivery of individual datagrams with no connection required beforehand. An application choosing between them is choosing a service model, not choosing a set of implementation techniques, even though in practice choosing TCP also means inheriting its underlying mechanics like sequence numbers and retransmission.

Framing connection oriented versus connectionless, and best effort versus reliable delivery, as different service models rather than different protocols is what makes the distinctions transferable. The same tradeoff between guaranteed, ordered delivery and lightweight, unordered delivery reappears at other layers and in other systems entirely, from message queues to distributed databases, precisely because it is a property of the service being offered, not an accident specific to TCP and UDP.
